claim: The haptoglobin-haemoglobin receptor (HpHbR) of African trypanosomes allows acquisition of haem.
source: The haptoglobin-haemoglobin receptor (HpHbR) of African trypanosomes allows acquisition of haem and provides an uptake route for trypanolytic factor-1, a mediator of innate immunity against trypanosome infection.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known function of the receptor, supported by established scientific knowledge about trypanosome biology.

claim: The haptoglobin-haemoglobin receptor provides an uptake route for trypanolytic factor-1.
source: The haptoglobin-haemoglobin receptor (HpHbR) of African trypanosomes allows acquisition of haem and provides an uptake route for trypanolytic factor-1, a mediator of innate immunity against trypanosome infection.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known function of the receptor, supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: Trypanolytic factor-1 is a mediator of innate immunity against trypanosome infection.
source: The haptoglobin-haemoglobin receptor (HpHbR) of African trypanosomes allows acquisition of haem and provides an uptake route for trypanolytic factor-1, a mediator of innate immunity against trypanosome infection.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about TLF1 function.

claim: The structure of Trypanosoma brucei HpHbR in complex with human haptoglobin-haemoglobin was determined.
source: In this study, we report the structure of Trypanosoma brucei HpHbR in complex with human haptoglobin-haemoglobin (HpHb), revealing an elongated ligand-binding site that extends along its membrane distal half.
evidence: The abstract reports the determination of this structure as a primary finding of the study.

claim: The ligand-binding site of TbHpHbR is elongated and extends along its membrane distal half.
source: In this study, we report the structure of Trypanosoma brucei HpHbR in complex with human haptoglobin-haemoglobin (HpHb), revealing an elongated ligand-binding site that extends along its membrane distal half.
evidence: This structural feature is directly observed in the crystal structure reported in the study.

claim: The TbHpHbR ligand-binding site contacts haptoglobin and the β-subunit of haemoglobin.
source: This contacts haptoglobin and the β-subunit of haemoglobin, showing how the receptor selectively binds HpHb over individual components.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure of the complex.

claim: The receptor selectively binds HpHb over individual components due to contacts with both haptoglobin and the β-subunit of haemoglobin.
source: This contacts haptoglobin and the β-subunit of haemoglobin, showing how the receptor selectively binds HpHb over individual components.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data showing dual binding sites.

claim: TbHpHbR has a ∼50° kink in the receptor structure.
source: Lateral mobility of the glycosylphosphatidylinositol-anchored HpHbR, and a ∼50o kink in the receptor, allows two receptors to simultaneously bind one HpHb dimer.
evidence: This structural feature is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The ∼50° kink in TbHpHbR allows two receptors to simultaneously bind one HpHb dimer.
source: Lateral mobility of the glycosylphosphatidylinositol-anchored HpHbR, and a ∼50o kink in the receptor, allows two receptors to simultaneously bind one HpHb dimer.
evidence: This is supported by structural modeling and SAXS data showing the 2:1 receptor:ligand complex.

claim: Trypanosomes take up dimeric HpHb at significantly lower concentrations than monomeric HpHb.
source: Indeed, trypanosomes take up dimeric HpHb at significantly lower concentrations than monomeric HpHb, due to increased ligand avidity that comes from bivalent binding.
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry uptake experiments comparing HpHb and HpSPHb.

claim: Increased ligand avidity from bivalent binding causes more efficient uptake of dimeric HpHb compared to monomeric HpHb.
source: Indeed, trypanosomes take up dimeric HpHb at significantly lower concentrations than monomeric HpHb, due to increased ligand avidity that comes from bivalent binding.
evidence: This is inferred from the uptake data showing differential efficiency and the structural data showing 2:1 binding.

claim: African Animal Trypanosomiasis is one of the major constraints on the productivity of pastoralists in sub-Saharan Africa.
source: African Animal Trypanosomiasis is one of the major constraints on the productivity of pastoralists in sub-Saharan Africa and can be caused by infection by a range of trypanosome species (Shaw, 2004), while infections of humans are caused by only two subspecies of Trypanosoma brucei (Laveran, 1902; Pays and Vanhollebeke, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Shaw, 2004.

claim: African Animal Trypanosomiasis can be caused by infection by a range of trypanosome species.
source: African Animal Trypanosomiasis is one of the major constraints on the productivity of pastoralists in sub-Saharan Africa and can be caused by infection by a range of trypanosome species (Shaw, 2004), while infections of humans are caused by only two subspecies of Trypanosoma brucei (Laveran, 1902; Pays and Vanhollebeke, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Shaw, 2004.

claim: Infections of humans are caused by only two subspecies of Trypanosoma brucei.
source: African Animal Trypanosomiasis is one of the major constraints on the productivity of pastoralists in sub-Saharan Africa and can be caused by infection by a range of trypanosome species (Shaw, 2004), while infections of humans are caused by only two subspecies of Trypanosoma brucei (Laveran, 1902; Pays and Vanhollebeke, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Laveran, 1902 and Pays and Vanhollebeke, 2009.

claim: The trypanosome disease is persistent as the host immune system is usually unable to clear the infection.
source: The disease is persistent as the host immune system is usually unable to clear the infection.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about trypanosome infections.

claim: The trypanosome has evolved a population survival strategy based on autoregulation of parasitaemia and antigenic variation.
source: This is due to the trypanosome having evolved a population survival strategy based on autoregulation of parasitaemia and antigenic variation (MacGregor et al., 2011; Horn, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to MacGregor et al., 2011 and Horn, 2014.

claim: Trypanosomes internalize and degrade surface bound immunoglobulin.
source: The trypanosomes also internalize and degrade surface bound immunoglobulin (Pal et al., 2003; Engstler et al., 2007), increasing the survival of an individual cell and thereby increasing the likelihood of transmission.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pal et al., 2003 and Engstler et al., 2007.

claim: Internalization and degradation of surface bound immunoglobulin increases the survival of an individual trypanosome cell.
source: The trypanosomes also internalize and degrade surface bound immunoglobulin (Pal et al., 2003; Engstler et al., 2007), increasing the survival of an individual cell and thereby increasing the likelihood of transmission.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited studies on immunoglobulin degradation.

claim: Internalization and degradation of surface bound immunoglobulin increases the likelihood of trypanosome transmission.
source: The trypanosomes also internalize and degrade surface bound immunoglobulin (Pal et al., 2003; Engstler et al., 2007), increasing the survival of an individual cell and thereby increasing the likelihood of transmission.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased survival of individual cells.

claim: Trypanosomes have a densely packed cell surface coat of variant surface glycoprotein (VSG).
source: Both of these strategies require a densely packed cell surface coat of variant surface glycoprotein (VSG) that acts as a barrier, preventing access of host immunoglobulins to the plasma membrane (Schwede and Carrington, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schwede and Carrington, 2010.

claim: The VSG coat acts as a barrier, preventing access of host immunoglobulins to the plasma membrane.
source: Both of these strategies require a densely packed cell surface coat of variant surface glycoprotein (VSG) that acts as a barrier, preventing access of host immunoglobulins to the plasma membrane (Schwede and Carrington, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schwede and Carrington, 2010.

claim: The VSG coat undergoes antigenic variation through expression of a single VSG gene from a genomic repertoire of hundreds.
source: This coat also undergoes antigenic variation through expression of a single VSG gene from a genomic repertoire of hundreds (Horn, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Horn, 2014.

claim: The VSG coat must be permissive for receptor-mediated binding and uptake of macromolecular ligands.
source: Although the VSG coat restricts immunoglobulin access, it must be permissive for receptor-mediated binding and uptake of macromolecular ligands.
evidence: This is inferred from the need for nutrient uptake despite the protective coat.

claim: T. brucei has receptors for transferrin (TfR) for iron.
source: T. brucei, and the closely related T. congolense, have receptors for both transferrin (TfR) for iron (Steverding et al., 1994; Schell et al., 1991; Jackson et al., 2013) and haptoglobin-haemoglobin (HpHbR) for haem (Vanhollebeke et al., 2008; Higgins et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Steverding et al., 1994; Schell et al., 1991; Jackson et al., 2013.

claim: T. brucei has receptors for haptoglobin-haemoglobin (HpHbR) for haem.
source: T. brucei, and the closely related T. congolense, have receptors for both transferrin (TfR) for iron (Steverding et al., 1994; Schell et al., 1991; Jackson et al., 2013) and haptoglobin-haemoglobin (HpHbR) for haem (Vanhollebeke et al., 2008; Higgins et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Vanhollebeke et al., 2008; Higgins et al., 2013.

claim: T. congolense has receptors for transferrin (TfR) for iron.
source: T. brucei, and the closely related T. congolense, have receptors for both transferrin (TfR) for iron (Steverding et al., 1994; Schell et al., 1991; Jackson et al., 2013) and haptoglobin-haemoglobin (HpHbR) for haem (Vanhollebeke et al., 2008; Higgins et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Steverding et al., 1994; Schell et al., 1991; Jackson et al., 2013.

claim: T. congolense has receptors for haptoglobin-haemoglobin (HpHbR) for haem.
source: T. brucei, and the closely related T. congolense, have receptors for both transferrin (TfR) for iron (Steverding et al., 1994; Schell et al., 1991; Jackson et al., 2013) and haptoglobin-haemoglobin (HpHbR) for haem (Vanhollebeke et al., 2008; Higgins et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Vanhollebeke et al., 2008; Higgins et al., 2013.

claim: Trypanosome receptors are held on the external face of the plasma membrane by covalent attachment of the C-terminal carboxyl group to a glycosylphosphatidyl inositol to form a GPI-anchor.
source: These are held on the external face of the plasma membrane by covalent attachment of the C-terminal carboxyl group to a glycosylphosphatidyl inositol to form a GPI-anchor.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about trypanosome receptor anchoring.

claim: Trypanosome receptors have free movement in the lateral plane of the membrane.
source: All have free movement in the lateral plane of the membrane, although the receptors are concentrated in the flagellar pocket, an invagination of the plasma membrane at the base of the flagellum and the site of all endocytosis (Mussmann et al., 2004; Vanhollebeke et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mussmann et al., 2004; Vanhollebeke et al., 2008.

claim: Trypanosome receptors are concentrated in the flagellar pocket.
source: All have free movement in the lateral plane of the membrane, although the receptors are concentrated in the flagellar pocket, an invagination of the plasma membrane at the base of the flagellum and the site of all endocytosis (Mussmann et al., 2004; Vanhollebeke et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mussmann et al., 2004; Vanhollebeke et al., 2008.

claim: The flagellar pocket is an invagination of the plasma membrane at the base of the flagellum and the site of all endocytosis.
source: All have free movement in the lateral plane of the membrane, although the receptors are concentrated in the flagellar pocket, an invagination of the plasma membrane at the base of the flagellum and the site of all endocytosis (Mussmann et al., 2004; Vanhollebeke et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mussmann et al., 2004; Vanhollebeke et al., 2008.

claim: Humans display innate immunity to most trypanosome species through the action of trypanolytic factors-1 and -2 (TLF1 and TLF2).
source: Humans, together with a few other primates, display innate immunity to most trypanosome species (Laveran, 1902) through the action of trypanolytic factors-1 and -2 (TLF1 and TLF2) (Hager et al., 1994; Raper et al., 1996, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Laveran, 1902; Hager et al., 1994; Raper et al., 1996, 1999.

claim: A few other primates display innate immunity to most trypanosome species through the action of trypanolytic factors-1 and -2.
source: Humans, together with a few other primates, display innate immunity to most trypanosome species (Laveran, 1902) through the action of trypanolytic factors-1 and -2 (TLF1 and TLF2) (Hager et al., 1994; Raper et al., 1996, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Laveran, 1902; Hager et al., 1994; Raper et al., 1996, 1999.

claim: TLF1 and TLF2 both include apolipoprotein L1 (ApoL1) together with complexes of haemoglobin bound to haptoglobin-related protein (HprHb).
source: Although containing different scaffold components, these factors both include apolipoprotein L1 (ApoL1) together with complexes of haemoglobin bound to haptoglobin-related protein (HprHb) (Vanhamme et al., 2003; Pérez-Morga et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Vanhamme et al., 2003; Pérez-Morga et al., 2005.

claim: TLF1 enters trypanosomes via receptor-mediated endocytosis, through binding of the HprHb component to HpHbR.
source: TLF1 enters trypanosomes via receptor-mediated endocytosis, through binding of the HprHb component to HpHbR (Drain et al., 2001; Widener et al., 2007; Vanhollebeke et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Drain et al., 2001; Widener et al., 2007; Vanhollebeke et al., 2008.

claim: TLF1 delivers ApoL1 to the endosome where it causes lysosomal swelling and cell death.
source: This delivers ApoL1 to the endosome where it causes lysosomal swelling and cell death (Pérez-Morga et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pérez-Morga et al., 2005.

claim: The uptake route for TLF2 is unclear.
source: In contrast, the uptake route for TLF2 is unclear as, unlike TLF1, it is able to kill HpHbR null mutants (Capewell et al., 2013; Uzureau et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Capewell et al., 2013; Uzureau et al., 2013.

claim: TLF2 is able to kill HpHbR null mutants.
source: In contrast, the uptake route for TLF2 is unclear as, unlike TLF1, it is able to kill HpHbR null mutants (Capewell et al., 2013; Uzureau et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Capewell et al., 2013; Uzureau et al., 2013.

claim: Two subspecies of T. brucei (T. b. rhodesiense and T. b. gambiense) have evolved counter measures to the trypanolytic factors.
source: Just two subspecies of T. brucei (T. b. rhodesiense and T. b. gambiense) have evolved counter measures to the trypanolytic factors, allowing them to cause Human African Trypanosomiasis (Pays et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pays et al., 2014.

claim: T. b. rhodesiense and T. b. gambiense cause Human African Trypanosomiasis.
source: Just two subspecies of T. brucei (T. b. rhodesiense and T. b. gambiense) have evolved counter measures to the trypanolytic factors, allowing them to cause Human African Trypanosomiasis (Pays et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pays et al., 2014.

claim: Human-infective group 1 T. b. gambiense has a unique point polymorphism in HpHbR.
source: In the case of human-infective group 1 T. b. gambiense, a unique point polymorphism is found in HpHbR (Symula et al., 2012) that reduces the monovalent affinity for ligand by 20-fold (Higgins et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Symula et al., 2012 and Higgins et al., 2013.

claim: The unique point polymorphism in T. b. gambiense HpHbR reduces the monovalent affinity for ligand by 20-fold.
source: In the case of human-infective group 1 T. b. gambiense, a unique point polymorphism is found in HpHbR (Symula et al., 2012) that reduces the monovalent affinity for ligand by 20-fold (Higgins et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Higgins et al., 2013.

claim: The point polymorphism in T. b. gambiense HpHbR contributes to resistance to TLF1.
source: This contributes to resistance to TLF1, illustrating the importance of HpHbR.
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced affinity for ligand.

claim: Haptoglobin-haemoglobin is an elongated 'dumbell-shaped' complex consisting of a dimer of haptoglobin molecules, each joined to an αβ haemoglobin dimer.
source: Haptoglobin-haemoglobin is an elongated 'dumbell-shaped' complex consisting of a dimer of haptoglobin molecules, each joined to an αβ haemoglobin dimer (Andersen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Andersen et al., 2012.

claim: Trypanosomes take up the HpHb complex but not the individual components.
source: Trypanosomes take up this HpHb complex but not the individual components (Vanhollebeke et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vanhollebeke et al., 2008.

claim: The structure of the T. congolense HpHbR is an elongated three-helical bundle with a small membrane distal head.
source: The structure of the T. congolense HpHbR is an elongated three-helical bundle with a small membrane distal head (Higgins et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Higgins et al., 2013.

claim: Residues involved in HpHb binding in T. congolense HpHbR are part of a small conserved patch ∼25 Å below the tip of the receptor.
source: Residues involved in HpHb binding are part of a small conserved patch ∼25 Å below the tip of the receptor, but details of ligand binding and uptake were not characterized.
evidence: This is stated as prior knowledge from previous structural studies.

claim: TbHpHbR adopts a similar architecture to its T. congolense homologue.
source: We show that the receptor adopts a similar architecture to its T. congolense homologue, but with a ∼50° kink a third of the way along from the membrane proximal end.
evidence: This is observed by comparing the crystal structures of the two receptors.

claim: TbHpHbR has a ∼50° kink a third of the way along from the membrane proximal end.
source: We show that the receptor adopts a similar architecture to its T. congolense homologue, but with a ∼50° kink a third of the way along from the membrane proximal end.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The kink in TbHpHbR allows efficient ligand uptake in the context of the tightly packed VSG coat.
source: This reveals the molecular basis for the uptake of HpHb and trypanolytic factor-1 and identifies adaptations in the trypanosome receptor that allow efficient ligand uptake in the context of the tightly packed VSG coat.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural and functional data showing bivalent binding and increased uptake efficiency.

claim: TbHpHbR is longer than its homologue from T. congolense due to the presence of an additional C-terminal membrane-proximal domain.
source: TbHpHbR is longer than its homologue from T. congolense due to the presence of an additional C-terminal membrane-proximal domain.
evidence: This is stated as a known difference between the two receptors.

claim: The region of TbHpHbR corresponding to T. congolense HpHbR is residues 36–299.
source: We therefore used the previously determined structure of T. congolense HpHbR (Higgins et al., 2013) to design a construct containing the corresponding region of TbHpHbR (residues 36–299).
evidence: This is stated as the construct design used in the study.

claim: The region of TbHpHbR used in this study is identical in the human infective T. b. rhodesiense.
source: This region of the protein is identical in the human infective T. b. rhodesiense.
evidence: This is stated as a known sequence identity.

claim: Haptoglobin-haemoglobin consists of a dimer of haptoglobin chains, each interacting with an αβ dimer of haemoglobin, and adopts a dimeric 'dumbell-shaped' architecture.
source: Haptoglobin-haemoglobin consists of a dimer of haptoglobin chains, each interacting with an αβ dimer of haemoglobin, and adopts a dimeric 'dumbell-shaped' architecture (Andersen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Andersen et al., 2012.

claim: At each end of HpHb, a serine protease (HpSP) domain of haptoglobin forms a stable complex with a haemoglobin dimer.
source: At each end, a serine protease (HpSP) domain of haptoglobin forms a stable complex with a haemoglobin dimer.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about HpHb structure.

claim: Dimerisation of HpHb occurs through an interface formed by the CCP domains of haptoglobin.
source: Dimerisation occurs through an interface formed by the CCP domains of haptoglobin, linking together these HpSPHb 'heads'.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about HpHb structure.

claim: TbHpHbR interacts with the HpHb complex but not with either haptoglobin or haemoglobin alone.
source: Previous studies have shown that TbHpHbR interacts with the HpHb complex but not with either haptoglobin or haemoglobin alone (Vanhollebeke et al., 2008), suggesting that that the receptor most likely binds to the heads of HpHb, where its two constituent components come together.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vanhollebeke et al., 2008.

claim: The receptor most likely binds to the heads of HpHb, where its two constituent components come together.
source: Previous studies have shown that TbHpHbR interacts with the HpHb complex but not with either haptoglobin or haemoglobin alone (Vanhollebeke et al., 2008), suggesting that that the receptor most likely binds to the heads of HpHb, where its two constituent components come together.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the receptor requires both components for binding.

claim: HpSPHb complexes bind to TbHpHbR with an affinity of 0.7 μM.
source: We used surface plasmon resonance to determine the affinity of these HpSPHb complexes for TbHpHbR, and showed binding with an affinity of 0.7 μM (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), similar to the 1 μM affinity observed for intact human HpHb (Higgins et al., 2013).
evidence: This is measured by surface plasmon resonance experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The affinity of HpSPHb for TbHpHbR is similar to the 1 μM affinity observed for intact human HpHb.
source: We used surface plasmon resonance to determine the affinity of these HpSPHb complexes for TbHpHbR, and showed binding with an affinity of 0.7 μM (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), similar to the 1 μM affinity observed for intact human HpHb (Higgins et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Higgins et al., 2013 and the SPR data in this study.

claim: Proteolytic cleavage of haptoglobin normally occurs in the endoplasmic reticulum after residue R102.
source: Proteolytic cleavage of haptoglobin normally occurs in the endoplasmic reticulum after residue R102 but this cleavage event did not occur in the insect cell expressed HpSP domain.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about haptoglobin processing.

claim: Proteolytic cleavage of haptoglobin did not occur in the insect cell expressed HpSP domain.
source: Proteolytic cleavage of haptoglobin normally occurs in the endoplasmic reticulum after residue R102 but this cleavage event did not occur in the insect cell expressed HpSP domain.
evidence: This is observed in the expression system used in the study.

claim: The lack of proteolytic cleavage in insect cell expressed HpSP did not affect the affinity for TbHpHbR.
source: However, this did not affect the affinity for TbHpHbR.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the similar affinities measured for cleaved and uncleaved forms.

claim: The shortened TbHpHbR construct and the HpSPHb complex interact together with the same affinity as the full-length components.
source: The shortened TbHpHbR construct and the HpSPHb complex therefore interact together with the same affinity as the full-length components, providing reagents for structural determination.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the SPR measurements comparing truncated and full-length forms.

claim: TbHpHbR binds to the 'head' structure of dimeric HpHb.
source: These findings also confirm that TbHpHbR binds to the 'head' structure of dimeric HpHb, raising the possibility of two receptors simultaneously interacting with one HpHb complex.
evidence: This is confirmed by the binding studies with HpSPHb.

claim: Two receptors can simultaneously interact with one HpHb complex.
source: These findings also confirm that TbHpHbR binds to the 'head' structure of dimeric HpHb, raising the possibility of two receptors simultaneously interacting with one HpHb complex.
evidence: This is inferred from the binding to the head structure and the dimeric nature of HpHb.

claim: Crystals of HpSPHb diffracted to 2.05 Å.
source: Crystals of HpSPHb diffracted to 2.05 Å and were of space group P3121 with one complex in the asymmetric unit.
evidence: This is reported from the crystallographic data collection.

claim: Crystals of HpSPHb were of space group P3121 with one complex in the asymmetric unit.
source: Crystals of HpSPHb diffracted to 2.05 Å and were of space group P3121 with one complex in the asymmetric unit.
evidence: This is reported from the crystallographic data collection.

claim: Crystals of TbHpHbR diffracted to 1.85 Å resolution.
source: Crystals of TbHpHbR diffracted to 1.85 Å resolution and were of space group P21 with two molecules in the asymmetric unit.
evidence: This is reported from the crystallographic data collection.

claim: Crystals of TbHpHbR were of space group P21 with two molecules in the asymmetric unit.
source: Crystals of TbHpHbR diffracted to 1.85 Å resolution and were of space group P21 with two molecules in the asymmetric unit.
evidence: This is reported from the crystallographic data collection.

claim: Crystals of the TbHpHbR:HpSPHb complex were of space group C2 and diffracted to 3.1 Å resolution with a single complex in the asymmetric unit.
source: Crystals of the TbHpHbR:HpSPHb complex were of space group C2 and diffracted to 3.1 Å resolution with a single complex in the asymmetric unit (Table 1).
evidence: This is reported from the crystallographic data collection.

claim: TbHpHbR is elongated, consisting primarily of a three-helical bundle with a total length of 118 Å.
source: Like T. congolense HpHbR, the T. brucei receptor is elongated, consisting primarily of a three-helical bundle (Figure 1): helix I (red; residues 42–110), helix II (orange; residues 116–182), and helix V (dark blue; residues 224–296) with a total length of 118 Å.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 1.

claim: At the membrane distal end, TbHpHbR widens to form a compact head structure that includes the N-terminus and a 42-residue loop containing two further helices.
source: At the membrane distal end, the receptor widens to form a compact head structure that includes the N-terminus and a 42-residue loop containing two further helices, helix III (yellow: residues 186–196) and helix IV (green: residues 207-–218).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The upper part of TbHpHbR is extremely similar to that from T. congolense, with the membrane distal halves of the two receptors aligning with a root mean square deviation of 1.1 Å.
source: The upper part of the structure is extremely similar to that from T. congolense, with the membrane distal halves of the two receptors aligning with a root mean square deviation of 1.1 Å (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is determined by structural alignment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The kink in TbHpHbR is not caused by flexibility, but is a rigid feature of the receptor.
source: This kink is not caused by flexibility, but is a rigid feature of the receptor, as it adopts the same confirmation in crystals of receptor alone, and in crystals of its complex with HpSPHb (Figure 2A), and is also observed in molecular envelopes derived from small angle x-ray scattering (Figure 1, Table 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by observing the same kink in multiple crystal forms and in SAXS data.

claim: The kink in TbHpHbR is caused by changes in the pattern of hydrophobic and hydrophilic residues around the kink site in each of the three helices.
source: Instead it is caused by changes in the pattern of hydrophobic and hydrophilic residues around the kink site in each of the three helices.
evidence: This is inferred from structural analysis of the residues at the kink site.

claim: The three long helices of the T. congolense receptor are characterised by an alternating pattern of hydrophobic and hydrophilic residues.
source: The three long helices of the T. congolense receptor are characterised by an alternating pattern of hydrophobic and hydrophilic residues, leading to continuous hydrophobic strips along the length of each helix that pack in the core of the helical bundle, stabilising its fold.
evidence: This is observed from structural analysis of T. congolense HpHbR.

claim: In the T. brucei receptor, the pattern of hydrophobic and hydrophilic residues is disturbed at each kink site, breaking the organisation of the helix.
source: In the T. brucei receptor, this pattern is disturbed at each kink site, breaking the organisation of the helix and leading to an alteration in the surface that displays the hydrophobic patch (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is observed from structural analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The disturbance in the pattern of hydrophobic residues stabilises the kink and makes it a rigid feature of the receptor structure.
source: This stabilises the kink and makes it a rigid feature of the receptor structure.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural analysis of the kink region.

claim: The haptoglobin-haemoglobin complex covers a total area of ∼1250 Å2 of the receptor.
source: The haptoglobin-haemoglobin complex covers a total area of ∼1250 Å2 of the receptor and can be divided into two distinct regions (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is calculated from the crystal structure of the complex.

claim: The membrane distal part of the binding site (∼745 Å2) contacts the β-subunit of the haemoglobin dimer with no contacts between the receptor and the haemoglobin α-subunit.
source: The membrane distal part, (∼745 Å2) contacts the β-subunit of the haemoglobin dimer with no contacts between the receptor and the haemoglobin α-subunit.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure of the complex.

claim: The membrane proximal region of the binding site (∼505 Å2) forms a binding surface for haptoglobin.
source: The membrane proximal region (∼505 Å2) forms a binding surface for haptoglobin.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure of the complex.

claim: The involvement of both haemoglobin and haptoglobin in binding explains why the receptor binds HpHb but not haptoglobin alone.
source: The involvement of both haemoglobin and haptoglobin in binding explains why the receptor binds HpHb but not haptoglobin alone.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observation of dual binding sites.

claim: The lack of haemoglobin binding is due to steric clashes of the receptor with the second αβ dimer of haemoglobin when the β-subunit of a haemoglobin tetramer is docked onto the receptor.
source: Modelling suggests that the lack of haemoglobin binding is due to steric clashes of the receptor with the second αβ dimer of haemoglobin when the β-subunit of a haemoglobin tetramer is docked onto the receptor with the binding mode observed in the TbHpHbR:HpSPHb complex (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by molecular modeling shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The conformation of the receptor and the presence of two distinct binding sites allow the receptor to specifically select HpHb over its two constitutive components.
source: Therefore, the conformation of the receptor and the presence of two distinct binding sites allow the receptor to specifically select HpHb over its two constitutive components.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural and modeling data.

claim: The haemoglobin β-subunit makes a number of direct interactions, mostly hydrogen bonds, with the receptor.
source: The haemoglobin β-subunit makes a number of direct interactions, mostly hydrogen bonds, with the receptor (Figure 2C, Table 4).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure and detailed in Table 4.

claim: Side chains from helix I of the receptor make the majority of contacts with haemoglobin.
source: Side chains from helix I of the receptor make the majority of these contacts, with additional interactions from helix II and the loop that links helices III and IV.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure of the complex.

claim: The haem group makes direct contacts with the receptor, with the propionate chains contacting residues K56, S59, K164, R199 and Y200 of the receptor.
source: The haem group also makes direct contacts with the receptor, with the propionate chains contacting residues K56, S59, K164, R199 and Y200 of the receptor.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure of the complex.

claim: Interactions mediated by haem form ∼140 Å2 of the ∼745 Å2 total contact area of Hb.
source: These interactions, mediated by haem, form ∼140 Å2 of the ∼745 Å2 total contact area of Hb.
evidence: This is calculated from the crystal structure of the complex.

claim: The haptoglobin subunit interacts with helix I of the receptor through a predominantly hydrophobic contact.
source: The haptoglobin subunit also interacts with helix I of the receptor, through a predominantly hydrophobic contact, mediated by three loops that emerge from the C-terminal β-sheet of haptoglobin (Figure 2B, Table 4).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure and detailed in Table 4.

claim: The structure of human haptoglobin from this complex aligns with that from porcine Hp with a root mean square deviation of just 0.5 Å.
source: The structure of human haptoglobin from this complex aligns with that from porcine Hp with a root mean square deviation of just 0.5 Å and reveals no significant structural change on receptor binding (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is determined by structural alignment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: There is no significant structural change in haptoglobin on receptor binding.
source: The structure of human haptoglobin from this complex aligns with that from porcine Hp with a root mean square deviation of just 0.5 Å and reveals no significant structural change on receptor binding (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is observed by comparing structures before and after binding.

claim: The natural cleavage of Hp does not affect TbHpHbR binding, as residues in the loop that contains the cleavage site are not close to the receptor.
source: The alignment also confirms that the natural cleavage of Hp does not affect TbHpHbR binding, as residues in the loop that contains the cleavage site are not close to the receptor.
evidence: This is confirmed by structural analysis and SPR data.

claim: Trypanolytic factor-1 (TLF1) contains haptoglobin-related protein (Hpr) rather than haptoglobin.
source: Rather than haptoglobin, trypanolytic factor-1 (TLF1) contains haptoglobin-related protein (Hpr) and binding of HprHb complex to TbHpHbR results in TLF1 uptake.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about TLF1 composition.

claim: Binding of HprHb complex to TbHpHbR results in TLF1 uptake.
source: Rather than haptoglobin, trypanolytic factor-1 (TLF1) contains haptoglobin-related protein (Hpr) and binding of HprHb complex to TbHpHbR results in TLF1 uptake.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about TLF1 uptake mechanism.

claim: The HprSP domain contains a total of sixteen amino acid substitutions when compared with the HpSP domain.
source: The HprSP domain contains a total of sixteen amino acid substitutions when compared with the HpSP domain.
evidence: This is determined by sequence comparison.

claim: None of the sixteen amino acid differences between HprSP and HpSP lie in residues that contact the receptor.
source: Mapping these onto the structure shows that none of these differences lie in residues that contact the receptor (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is observed by mapping sequence differences onto the structure shown in Figure 3A.

claim: HprSPHb complexes bound to the receptor with an affinity of 1.7 μM.
source: Indeed HprSPHb complexes, prepared using the same protocols as HpSPHb complexes, bound to the receptor with an affinity of 1.7 μM, as determined by surface plasmon resonance (Figure 3B), comparable to the 0.7 μM affinity of the receptor for HpSPHb.
evidence: This is measured by surface plasmon resonance shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The affinity of HprSPHb for TbHpHbR (1.7 μM) is comparable to the 0.7 μM affinity of the receptor for HpSPHb.
source: Indeed HprSPHb complexes, prepared using the same protocols as HpSPHb complexes, bound to the receptor with an affinity of 1.7 μM, as determined by surface plasmon resonance (Figure 3B), comparable to the 0.7 μM affinity of the receptor for HpSPHb.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing SPR measurements for both complexes.

claim: HprHb and TLF1 will have a shared binding mode with HpHb.
source: This suggests that HprHb, and as a result, TLF1, will have a shared binding mode with HpHb.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar affinities and lack of sequence differences at the binding interface.

claim: The location of the binding site for HpHb extends some 70 Å from the membrane distal tip of the receptor and below the surface of the VSG layer.
source: It is therefore initially surprising that the location of the binding site for bulky HpHb complexes extends some 70 Å from the membrane distal tip of the receptor and below the surface of the VSG layer.
evidence: This is observed from the crystal structure of the complex.

claim: The kink in the T. brucei receptor increases its effective diameter, pushing apart VSG molecules.
source: However, one consequence of the kink in the T. brucei receptor is to increase its effective diameter, pushing apart VSG molecules.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural geometry of the kinked receptor.

claim: The orientation of the kink is precisely arranged to increase exposure of the HpHb binding site to the surface.
source: In addition, the orientation of the kink is precisely arranged to increase exposure of the HpHb binding site to the surface, making it more accessible for ligand binding.
evidence: This is inferred from structural analysis of the kink orientation.

claim: Docking of TbHpHbR:HpSPHb structures onto the structure of dimeric porcine HpHb suggests that two receptors can bind simultaneously to a single HpHb dimer.
source: Docking of TbHpHbR:HpSPHb structures onto the structure of dimeric porcine HpHb reveals another consequence of the kink. This modelling suggests that two receptors can bind simultaneously to a single HpHb dimer, resulting in a C-shaped complex with a parallel arrangement of the membrane proximal parts of the two receptors (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by molecular modeling shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Two receptors binding to one HpHb results in a C-shaped complex with a parallel arrangement of the membrane proximal parts of the two receptors.
source: This modelling suggests that two receptors can bind simultaneously to a single HpHb dimer, resulting in a C-shaped complex with a parallel arrangement of the membrane proximal parts of the two receptors (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by molecular modeling shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Small angle x-ray scattering confirmed the assembly of a complex containing two receptors and one HpHb in vitro.
source: Indeed, this arrangement was confirmed in solution by small angle x-ray scattering. Native (dimeric) human HpHb was mixed with TbHpHbR, and gel filtration was performed, with SAXS data collected from samples as they emerged from the column. The resultant scattering curves confirmed the assembly of a complex containing two receptors and one HpHb in vitro.
evidence: This is demonstrated by SAXS experiments.

claim: SAXS data generated a molecular envelope for the TbHpHbR:HpHb complex that confirmed the C-shaped architecture.
source: These data were used to generate a molecular envelope for the complex, which confirmed the C-shaped architecture (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Table 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SAXS analysis shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Multi-angle laser light scattering revealed masses of 30 kDa for the receptor, 150 kDa for HpHb and 210 kDa for the complex.
source: Additional support for the formation of this complex in solution came from multi-angle laser light scattering (SEC-MALLS), which revealed masses of 30 kDa for the receptor, 150 kDa for HpHb and 210 kDa for the complex, showing that two receptors bind to each HpHb in solution (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is measured by SEC-MALLS shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Two receptors bind to each HpHb in solution.
source: Additional support for the formation of this complex in solution came from multi-angle laser light scattering (SEC-MALLS), which revealed masses of 30 kDa for the receptor, 150 kDa for HpHb and 210 kDa for the complex, showing that two receptors bind to each HpHb in solution (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the molecular weight measurements by SEC-MALLS.

claim: Two independent GPI-anchored receptors can bind simultaneously to an HpHb dimer, which would increase avidity for the ligand and decrease the ligand concentration required for efficient uptake.
source: This arrangement, in which two independent GPI-anchored receptors can bind simultaneously to an HpHb dimer, would increase avidity for the ligand and decrease the ligand concentration required for efficient uptake.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural and biophysical data showing 2:1 binding.

claim: In wild-type T. brucei cells, uptake of HpHb reached saturation below a concentration of 4 nM.
source: In wild-type T. brucei cells, uptake of HpHb reached saturation below a concentration of 4 nM (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is measured by flow cytometry uptake experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The uptake of HpSPHb was negligible at a concentration of 4 nM and continued to increase at 62.5 nM.
source: In contrast, the uptake of HpSPHb was negligible at a concentration of 4 nM and continued to increase at 62.5 nM (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is measured by flow cytometry uptake experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Uptake of HpSPHb and HpHb observed in wild-type cells was due to the TbHpHbR.
source: Uptake of HpSPHb and HpHb observed in wild-type cells was due to the TbHpHbR, as expected (Vanhollebeke et al., 2008), as uptake of both ligands into TbHpHbR−/− cells was comparable to that of BSA in the range of ligand concentrations assayed (0–62.5 nM).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing uptake in wild-type and knockout cells, supported by citation to Vanhollebeke et al., 2008.

claim: Uptake of dimeric HpHb into trypanosomes occurs efficiently at a significantly lower concentration than that of monomeric HpSPHb.
source: Therefore, uptake of dimeric HpHb into trypanosomes occurs efficiently at a significantly lower concentration than that of monomeric HpSPHb.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the uptake experiments comparing HpHb and HpSPHb.

claim: The monovalent affinities of the receptor for HpHb and HpSPHb are indistinguishable.
source: As the monovalent affinities of the receptor for HpHb and HpSPHb are indistinguishable, as measured by surface plasmon resonance, this suggests that more efficient uptake of HpHb is caused by the dimeric ligand simultaneously binding to two receptors.
evidence: This is measured by surface plasmon resonance experiments.

claim: More efficient uptake of HpHb is caused by the dimeric ligand simultaneously binding to two receptors.
source: As the monovalent affinities of the receptor for HpHb and HpSPHb are indistinguishable, as measured by surface plasmon resonance, this suggests that more efficient uptake of HpHb is caused by the dimeric ligand simultaneously binding to two receptors.
evidence: This is inferred from the uptake data and the structural evidence for 2:1 binding.

claim: Measurements of the binding of HpHb to immobilised receptor using a very high surface density of HpHbR to measure bivalent binding gave an affinity of 4.5 nM.
source: Indeed, measurements of the binding of HpHb to immobilised receptor, using a very high surface density of HpHbR to measure bivalent binding, gave an affinity of 4.5 nM (Higgins et al., 2013), which is in the same range as the concentration at which HpHb uptake becomes saturated in live parasites.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Higgins et al., 2013.

claim: The bivalent binding affinity of 4.5 nM is in the same range as the concentration at which HpHb uptake becomes saturated in live parasites.
source: Indeed, measurements of the binding of HpHb to immobilised receptor, using a very high surface density of HpHbR to measure bivalent binding, gave an affinity of 4.5 nM (Higgins et al., 2013), which is in the same range as the concentration at which HpHb uptake becomes saturated in live parasites.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing the bivalent affinity with the uptake saturation concentration.

claim: TbHpHbR has evolved a kink to increase accessibility of its ligand-binding site and to allow simultaneous binding of two receptors to one HpHb ligand, increasing ligand avidity and uptake efficiency.
source: Therefore, it appears as though TbHpHbR has evolved a kink to increase accessibility of its ligand-binding site and to allow simultaneous binding of two receptors to one HpHb ligand, increasing ligand avidity and uptake efficiency.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural and functional data presented in the study.

claim: The external surface of an African trypanosome is covered with a tightly packed layer of variant surface glycoprotein that shields epitopes that lie close to the plasma membrane from antibody binding.
source: The external surface of an African trypanosome is covered with a tightly packed layer of variant surface glycoprotein that shields epitopes that lie close to the plasma membrane from antibody binding (Schwede et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schwede et al., 2011.

claim: Receptors required for the uptake of transferrin and haptoglobin-haemoglobin complexes must operate within the context of the VSG coat.
source: Receptors such as those required for the uptake of transferrin and haptoglobin-haemoglobin complexes must operate within the context of this coat, with their structures organised such that ligand binding sites are not masked by the VSG layer.
evidence: This is inferred from the need for nutrient uptake despite the protective VSG coat.

claim: The ligand-binding site of TbHpHbR extends more than half the way along the receptor, forming distinct binding surfaces for the β-subunit of haemoglobin and for haptoglobin.
source: Here, the first structure of a trypanosome receptor in complex with its ligand is presented: that of the T. brucei haptoglobin-haemoglobin receptor bound to haptoglobin-haemoglobin. Remarkably, the ligand-binding site extends more that half the way along the receptor, forming distinct binding surfaces for the β-subunit of haemoglobin and for haptoglobin.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure of the complex.

claim: The simultaneous binding of both haemoglobin and haptoglobin explains the specificity of the receptor for haptoglobin-haemoglobin complexes over each individual component.
source: The simultaneous binding of both components explains the specificity of the receptor for haptoglobin-haemoglobin complexes over each individual component.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observation of dual binding sites.

claim: The extent of the binding surface places it below the top of the VSG layer, apparently increasing the likelihood that it will be masked by VSG.
source: However, the extent of the binding surface places it below the top of the VSG layer, apparently increasing the likelihood that it will be masked by VSG.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural dimensions of the receptor and VSG layer.

claim: The direction of the kink is precisely arranged to bend the receptor such that the ligand-binding site becomes more exposed at the membrane surface.
source: However, a ∼50° rigid kink occurs as an adaptation in the three helical bundle of the T. brucei receptor, and we propose that it has two main functional consequences. Firstly, the direction of the kink is precisely arranged to bend the receptor such that the ligand-binding site becomes more exposed at the membrane surface.
evidence: This is inferred from structural analysis of the kink orientation.

claim: The kink will increase the separation of VSG molecules in the region of the receptor.
source: The kink will also increase the effective diameter of the receptor in the plane of the membrane. This combination is likely to increase the separation of VSG molecules in the region of the receptor and to increase the accessibility of the binding site for bulky macromolecular ligands such as HpHb and trypanolytic factors.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural geometry of the kinked receptor.

claim: Increased separation of VSG molecules by a trypanosome receptor is not a novel phenomena, with bulky glycan chains attached to the transferrin receptor proposed to have a similar effect.
source: Increased separation of VSG molecules by a trypanosome receptor is not a novel phenomena, with bulky glycan chains attached to the transferrin receptor proposed to have a similar effect (Mehlert et al., 2012), suggesting that different receptors increase the accessibility of binding sites for bulky ligands by different means.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mehlert et al., 2012.

claim: Different receptors increase the accessibility of binding sites for bulky ligands by different means.
source: Increased separation of VSG molecules by a trypanosome receptor is not a novel phenomena, with bulky glycan chains attached to the transferrin receptor proposed to have a similar effect (Mehlert et al., 2012), suggesting that different receptors increase the accessibility of binding sites for bulky ligands by different means.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing different receptor mechanisms.

claim: The receptor copy number is 200–400 and it is concentrated in the flagellar pocket.
source: The receptor copy number is 200–400 and it is concentrated in the flagellar pocket (Vanhollebeke et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vanhollebeke et al., 2008.

claim: The surface area of the flagellar pocket in live cells is 4.3 µm2.
source: The surface area of the flagellar pocket in live cells is 4.3 µm2 (Grünfelder et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Grünfelder et al., 2002.

claim: If there are 200 receptor molecules in the membrane of the flagellar pocket then the density is one receptor per 0.022 µm2.
source: If there are 200 receptor molecules in the membrane of the flagellar pocket then the density is one receptor per 0.022 µm2.
evidence: This is calculated from the receptor copy number and flagellar pocket surface area.

claim: The diffusion constant for VSG has been measured by fluorescence recovery after photobleaching to be 0.01 µm2/s.
source: The diffusion constant for HpHbR is unknown, but the diffusion constant for another GPI-anchored protein, VSG, has been measured by fluorescence recovery after photobleaching to be 0.01 µm2/s (Bulow et al., 1988); this means that the receptor will contact a receptor molecule approximately every 2 s.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bulow et al., 1988.

claim: The receptor will contact another receptor molecule approximately every 2 s.
source: The diffusion constant for HpHbR is unknown, but the diffusion constant for another GPI-anchored protein, VSG, has been measured by fluorescence recovery after photobleaching to be 0.01 µm2/s (Bulow et al., 1988); this means that the receptor will contact a receptor molecule approximately every 2 s.
evidence: This is calculated from the diffusion constant and receptor density.

claim: The t1/2 for release of monovalently bound HpHb is 70–100 s.
source: The t1/2 for release of monovalently bound HpHb is 70–100 s (Higgins et al., 2013) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), so if it is assumed that the receptor has a similar diffusion coefficient to the VSG, then it is very likely that a monovalently bound ligand will become bivalently bound.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Higgins et al., 2013 and SPR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: It is very likely that a monovalently bound ligand will become bivalently bound.
source: The t1/2 for release of monovalently bound HpHb is 70–100 s (Higgins et al., 2013) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), so if it is assumed that the receptor has a similar diffusion coefficient to the VSG, then it is very likely that a monovalently bound ligand will become bivalently bound.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the off-rate with the receptor encounter rate.

claim: Analysis of uptake of dimeric HpHb and monomeric HpSPHb into T. brucei confirmed that increased avidity occurs in vivo.
source: Indeed our analysis of uptake of dimeric HpHb and monomeric HpSPHb into T. brucei confirmed that this increased avidity does occur in vivo, with HpHb uptake saturating at a concentration below 4 nM, while HpSPHb uptake is far from saturation at 62.5 nM.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the uptake experiments.

claim: One mechanism used by human infective T. b. gambiense to avoid TLF1-mediated innate immunity is a point polymorphism in HpHbR that reduces the monovalent affinity for HpHb by 20-fold and reduces TLF1 uptake.
source: While the evolution of the kink allows increased accessibility of the binding site for HpHb, it would also increase accessibility for the large TLF1 complex. One mechanism used by human infective T. b. gambiense to avoid TLF1-mediated innate immunity is a point polymorphism in HpHbR that reduces the monovalent affinity for HpHb by 20-fold (Higgins et al., 2013) and reduces TLF1 uptake (Kieft et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Higgins et al., 2013 and Kieft et al., 2010.

claim: The T. congolense receptor lacks a kink.
source: As the kink in the receptor appears to have a number of functional consequences that facilitate ligand uptake, it is surprising that the T. congolense receptor lacks such a kink.
evidence: This is observed by comparing the structures of T. brucei and T. congolense receptors.

claim: T. congolense surface proteins lack a C-terminal domain.
source: One reason for this difference might be the lack of a C-terminal domain in T. congolense surface proteins (Higgins et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Higgins et al., 2013.

claim: The direct attachment of the ligand-binding domain to a GPI-anchor in T. congolense might provide enough flexibility to allow the receptors to adopt an angle that allows simultaneous uptake.
source: Perhaps the direct attachment of the ligand-binding domain to a GPI-anchor provides enough flexibility to allow the receptors to adopt an angle that allows simultaneous uptake, or perhaps the VSG coat of T. congolense parasites is less densely packed.
evidence: This is speculated as a possible explanation for the lack of kink in T. congolense.

claim: The VSG coat of T. congolense parasites might be less densely packed than that of T. brucei.
source: Perhaps the direct attachment of the ligand-binding domain to a GPI-anchor provides enough flexibility to allow the receptors to adopt an angle that allows simultaneous uptake, or perhaps the VSG coat of T. congolense parasites is less densely packed.
evidence: This is speculated as a possible explanation for the lack of kink in T. congolense.

claim: The structure reveals adaptations that decrease the packing of VSG molecules in the immediate vicinity of the receptor and increase accessibility of the ligand-binding site.
source: In conclusion, we present the first structure of a trypanosome receptor in complex with its ligand and reveal a number of adaptations that are tailored to facilitate efficient ligand binding in the context of the VSG coat. These will decrease the packing of VSG molecules in the immediate vicinity of the receptor and increase accessibility of the ligand-binding site.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural analysis of the kinked receptor.

claim: The adaptations allow two receptors to bind to a single ligand, thereby increasing avidity and dramatically decreasing the ligand concentration at which efficient uptake occurs.
source: They also allow two receptors to bind to a single ligand, thereby increasing avidity and dramatically decreasing the ligand concentration at which efficient uptake occurs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the structural and functional data showing 2:1 binding and increased uptake efficiency.

claim: Different adaptations might facilitate increased VSG separation and bivalent binding in different receptors, but these are expected to be general principles frequently used by the parasite to aid nutrient uptake and survival.
source: While different adaptations might facilitate each of these goals in different receptors, we would expect them to be general principles, frequently used by the parasite to aid nutrient uptake and survival.
evidence: This is speculated based on the findings for HpHbR.
